Washington (CNN) A conservative group filed a complaint against Sen. Claire McCaskill on Thursday, accusing her of violating federal campaign finance laws to beat Todd Akin in Missouri's 2012 Senate race.

The Foundation for Accountability and Civic Trust, a conservative government watchdog group, submitted a complaint to the Federal Election Commission saying that McCaskill attempted to illegally influence who would be her opponent in the Senate race by sharing valuable polling data with the Akin campaign.

"Senate McCaskill did not simply meddle in another party's primary, rather she crossed the legal line and made a prohibited donation in violation of federal law," said Matthew Whitaker, executive director of the group, in the complaint.

The complaint says McCaskill admitted to helping Akin win the Republican primary because she believed she could beat him in the general election. The Missouri senator wrote in a passage from her book "Plenty Ladylike" -- which was excerpted in Politico this week --- sharing how she spent $40,000 polling Missouri Republicans, and that staffers on the Akin campaign spoke with McCaskill's pollster.

Federal law limits in-kind campaign donations to $2,500, a figure the complaint says McCaskill violated by allowing her pollster to share data with the Akin campaign.

Main character, side character, a particular bad guy or villain. Which character in gaming do you find meaningful or interesting, and what is it about that character that makes them so compelling? Feel free to add to someone else's answer if there's something about their character that interests you. Let's kick off the weekend with some great gaming discussion!
Weekend Discussion: Think of a video game character who is particularly meaningful or interesting. What is it about that character that makes them so compelling?

I'm going to go with Master Chief. At first blush he seems like the stereotypical "man of few words" action hero, but I think it's how he uses his occasional dialog that makes him so interesting. He doesn't spit one-liners at the corpses of alien warriors, and he doesn't waste words where action will do. He's a stoic hero, but he cares about his comrades and stands up to authority when it questions the people he considers capable. He may not be the most complex machine on the outside, but he gives the impression that there's more going on under the hood than we realize.
Master Chief was always so interesting because of the mystery behind him. He was such a fearless hero with no face. I always wanted to be as tough and brave as John-117.

I think so too. The cool thing about silent protagonists is that it allows you to immerse yourself in the game and you feel like you've taken the place of the main character. I think that too much dialogue can pull you out of that. I think that both Half Life and Halo have done a great job of providing immersive story experiences with their use of non-player-character dialog, but I think that Halo has done the better job of still giving your character a personality despite the silence. Most of that comes from cut-scenes, where Half Life prefers to tell the story while you're playing, outside of cut-scenes. It's interesting how many different approaches there are to storytelling, and I'm glad that each developer brings their own take to storytelling.

I recently finished Talos Principle, so the one that's fresh in my mind is Alex, the girl behind the audio logs. The reason she's so good is she feels human, how she talks, what she talks about, it gives a truly human anchor in a game that asks the question of humanity. Her reactions to the events that transpire 'outside' of the game are incredibly well scripted and performed, and lend a very raw experience to what it means to be human.

There's probably a ton of others that are slipping my mind right now, I'll add on if I think of more.

I don't think I've played that game, but it sounds like she's meaningful because she's a character we can relate to. It's fun to play as a super soldier or larger than life hero, but sometimes the most compelling characters are also the most human.

1. Mordin Solus.

    Unlike most other characters, he understood the complexity of the issues the Normandy crew faced, and frequently acted through reason rather than emotion. Just as importantly, he often reflected on the difficult nature of the decisions we had made, thus giving us the impression of an actual internal struggle taking place within him. On top of that, he is one of the few scientists in gaming that actually behave and act in accordance with their title - he is very easily the most intelligent and well written character I've ever encountered in any game. My personal favorite, too.

  2. Solas.

    Solas resembles Mordin quite a bit, but due to the nature of the story surrounding his game series, the traits they share are expressed in some very different ways. Certain opinions remain the same - for example, they both feel that most folks are tragically irrational, and they have both been forced to take radical and controversial actions for the sake of the greater good. However, Solas' specific area of study includes an aspect of life that the vast majority of the people in his universe have come to misunderstand and abuse, meaning that he has seen some of the worst that life has to offer - such as the ruins of places that have been lost to the greed and ignorance of the mighty, and having to watch a dear friend being ripped from her realm and twisted to serve the petty purposes of weak men. This has hardened his view of humanity, and left him nearly fanatical in his pursuit and support of the rights of spirits. As if that wasn't enough, there's a scene at the end of DA:I that hints at the true complexity of his character, and the story surrounding him.

I like that you drew parallels between the two. It's interesting to see how different games write the "pragmatic scientist" type characters, and the inner conflict that it often entails. Great comment!

Geralt of Rivia. Not a gaming character per se, but it's how they made him a gaming character while remaining true to the books without breaking his established lore by using the most-overused and terrible trope ever: Amnesia.

The first game begins with Geralt lost in the woods and found by his brothers from Kaer Morhen, a Witcher's school. He doesn't know how he got there, but he has visions of the Wild Hunt, a wraith-like apparition that is said to be an omen of war, among other things. And with that amnesia, it allows the narrative to do several things that are crucially important but without doing anything out of character: It allows the world to be slowly introduced to the universe piece by piece without the main character already knowing everything and everyone, and it allows the player to role-play the character and make decisions that might be out of character for them.

On top of that, Geralt is simply an awesome character. He's a walking trope, he's the anti-hero bad-ass, stoic, wise-cracking, smart-ass, expert of death with superhuman abilities, but he's got character, beyond the basic gravelly voice, and you can't help but feel for him as he tries to do good and right but only to get shit on time and again by other characters and circumstances and just the nature of the world and the kingdoms he lives in and travels through.

So he's a good character, but it's how they made him a good character in an established universe and plonked him down in a way that let the player learn everything about him and make decisions for him without breaking anything that exists within that established universe that is really interesting to me.

It sounds like they made him a compelling character despite the initial clichés of his story and added a lot of depth to a character that could have been a much more shallow experience.
